messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Dentist
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 77

He is a quiet man, careful with his words. When he first came to my office, he sat on the edge of the chair, hands clasped, his gaze fixed somewhere past my shoulder. He is a dentist—fifty-eight years old, with steady hands and a practiced calm that he uses with his patients. But that calm, he tells me, is a mask. Inside, he is always watching, always scanning.

The event happened fourteen months ago. He had been driving home from his practice late on a Tuesday evening. A routine stop at a convenience store for coffee. As he walked back to his car, two plainclothes officers approached him. He does not remember why. He says he complied immediately—hands raised, no resistance. But the officers, he believes, mistook his motion for something else. One of them grabbed him, threw him face-first onto the hood of a parked car. The other pressed a knee into his back. He heard a voice shouting. He felt the cold metal of handcuffs. He thought he was going to die. The officers realized their mistake—wrong suspect—and released him with a curt apology. No charges. No explanation. He drove home in silence, his hands trembling on the wheel.

At first, he did not tell anyone. Not his partner, not his colleagues. He convinced himself it was a misunderstanding, that he should just move on. But the nightmares began that same week. He would wake in a sweat, convinced he was pinned down, unable to move. He started avoiding that part of town, then any drive after dark. He found himself scanning police cruisers, watching for officers in his peripheral vision. At his dental practice, he became short-tempered with hygienists who startled him. He once snapped at a patient for flinching during a procedure—an outburst so uncharacteristic that he had to step out of the room to compose himself.

His partner, a nurse, noticed the changes. He is distant, irritable. He stopped wanting to go out to dinner, to take their regular weekend walks. He says he feels like a stranger in his own life. The hypervigilance is constant. During my sessions, he often glances at the door. He flinches when I shift in my chair. He tells me that he cannot sit with his back to the entrance of a restaurant. He has stopped going to the gym because the locker room feels too enclosed. He cannot stand the feeling of being trapped.

The most painful part, he says, is the shame. He is a professional, a healer. He thinks of himself as a man who takes care of people, who solves problems. Now he struggles to concentrate on root canals, worried that his hands will shake. He has started double-checking every patient’s identity, replaying their names in his head, as if he might be accused of a mistake. He knows it is irrational, but the thought lingers.

The trauma replays in fragments. Not the whole memory, but snapshots: the pressure of the hood against his ribs, the gravel digging into his cheek, the voice shouting words he cannot quite hear. Sometimes he feels a phantom weight on his back. At night, he lies awake, unable to sleep, replaying what he could have done differently. He tells me that the world feels dangerous now, filled with unseen threats. Even his partner’s touch can startle him. He is living in a state of constant alert, exhausted but unable to rest.

He describes his life as before and after. Before, he was confident, easygoing, trusted his instincts. After, he is hollowed out, cautious, always bracing. He came here because his partner finally insisted, because he cannot keep pretending that everything is fine. In our sessions, he talks slowly, as if testing each word for safety. He is still a careful man—but now his carefulness is a cage.
